title: First opinion (Catharinus): private divine-faith certainty of one’s justification without special revelation
source_text: XV. Prima est eorum qui censent homines justos, sine speciali revelatione, habere posse de sua justificatione certitudinem fidei divinae, non Catholicae quidem, sed privatae. Ita sensit & docuit Ambrosius Catharinus, unus ex iis Episcopis quibus constitit Tridentina Synodus, cujus sententiam prolixe refert & explicat Vasquez in 1. 2. Tom. 2. Disp. 200. cap. 3. Ubi notat ex Catharino duobus modis haberi posse hunc fidei assensum de propria justificatione. Uno modo directe & proxime per revelationem Dei internam, & testimonium Spiritus Sancti, cui interius attestanti assentiamur: altero modo non ex directa revelatione, sed ex quibusdam certo revelatis, adjunctis aliis quae sensu percipiuntur, & experimento intra seipsum, homo didicit. Ut enim assensus aliquis censeatur esse divinae fidei, non opus esse revelationi proxime inniti, & ab ea solum oriri; sed sufficere, si colligatur ex principiis revelatis, junctis aliis quae experimento, aut alia ratione evidenter nota sunt. Atque hoc posteriori modo censuit Episcopus iste quemcunque justificatum certum esse posse divina fide privata se esse in gratia. Quia, scilicet, omnis adultus qui justificatur Catholica fide credit illum justificari, qui ad Sacramentum rite dispositus accedit, aut qui extra Sacramentum contritione & dilectione disponitur: hujus autem dispositionis habere potest quilibet justus evidens experimentum, adeoque potest etiam divina fide credere se justificatum esse. Porro dispositionem illam ad justificationem necessariam & sufficientem evidenter notam esse ipsi justificato, inde probat quia, nisi ita esset, sugillaretur divina providentia, quae requireret aliquid a nobis, quo ad gratiam remissionis peccatorum disponamur, ita occultum & absconditum ut nobis ipsis manifestum non sit. Adde quod necesse est ut stupidus ille sit, qui de se ipso nosse non potest, utrum ex animo & recta conscientia, an vero ficte ad Sacramentum accedat.
pass_a_gloss: The first is of those who judge that just persons, without special revelation, can have concerning their justification the certainty of divine faith—not indeed Catholic, but private. So felt and taught Ambrosius Catharinus, one of those bishops of whom the Tridentine Synod consisted, whose opinion Vasquez reports and explains at length in 1.2, volume 2, Disputation 200, chapter 3. Where he notes from Catharinus that this assent of faith concerning one’s own justification can be had in two ways. In one way directly and proximately through God’s internal revelation and the testimony of the Holy Spirit, to which attesting within we assent: in another way not from direct revelation, but from certain things certainly revealed, joined with others which are perceived by sense and which a person has learned by experience within himself. For that some assent may be counted as of divine faith, it need not rest proximately on revelation and arise from it alone; but it suffices if it is gathered from revealed principles joined with others that are evidently known by experience or another reason. And in this latter way that bishop judged that whoever is justified can be certain by private divine faith that he is in grace—because every adult who is justified believes by Catholic faith that he is justified who approaches the sacrament duly disposed, or who outside the sacrament is disposed by contrition and love; and of this disposition any just person can have evident experience, and therefore can also believe by divine faith that he has been justified. Further, that that disposition necessary and sufficient for justification is evidently known to the justified person himself he proves because, unless it were so, divine providence would be mocked, which would require something of us by which we are disposed to the grace of remission of sins, so hidden and concealed that it would not be manifest even to ourselves. Add that he must be stupid who cannot know of himself whether he approaches the sacrament from the heart and with a right conscience, or fictitiously.
pass_b_english: Catharinus allows private divine-faith certainty of being in grace without special revelation.
He argues that revealed sacramental principles plus evident experience of due disposition yield a divine-faith conclusion about one’s justification.
